one_liner: Young MIT libc subset in NASM/AVX2 and AArch64 NEON assembly; its arena and malloc heap beat glibc on burst workloads, string routines mostly parity.
what_it_does: A replacement for hot libc routines (memcpy/memset/memcmp/memchr, bounded string functions, strcmp/strcasecmp, strstr/memmem/strspn, ctype), plus a bump arena, an mmap-backed malloc heap, integer formatters, a printf family, a small sscanf, qsort/bsearch and a musl-derived freestanding libm, all behind one header (asmlib.h). Functions are named asm_* rather than replacing libc symbols; defining ASMLIB_ENABLE_LIBC_ALIASES maps many standard names onto them with macros. x86-64 (NASM, AVX2 with an IFUNC scalar fallback) and AArch64 (GNU as, NEON) share the API, and a portable C backend builds a no-import wasm32 module.
how_it_is_fast: The string/memory routines use 32-byte AVX2 compares with vpmovmskb/tzcnt, an eight-vector vpand fold in memcmp, aligned-down page-safe loads, two-byte candidate filtering in strstr/memmem, and a size-tiered memcpy (AVX2 below 96 KiB, ERMS rep movsb to 256 KiB, non-temporal stores above). The large published wins come from allocation models, not SIMD: the arena is a pointer bump with an O(chunks) reset, and asm_malloc is a segregated size-class slab heap with a lock-free per-thread cache that never returns small-run memory to the kernel. asm_u64toa emits digit groups from a 200-byte table with reciprocal multiplies, and asm_sscanf is a small branch-driven scanner covering only integers, %s, %c and %p.
when_to_use: Per-request or per-frame scratch allocation on Linux x86-64 or AArch64 where a bump arena with mark/release and bulk reset fits (published 8.6x to 19.8x over glibc malloc/free for 64 B to 512 B bursts)
Freestanding, -nostdlib or wasm32 builds that need a small libc subset plus libm with no imports
Hot integer-to-decimal conversion where asm_u64toa's bounded buffer API can replace snprintf("%llu") (20.32 vs 80.79 ns/call published)
Parsing simple integer or word fields with sscanf-like formats (2.2x to 3.1x published) when no floating point, scansets or %n are needed
As readable, heavily commented AVX2/NEON reference code for memchr/memcmp/strcasecmp-style kernels
when_not_to_use: Expecting faster memcpy/memset/strlen/strstr than glibc: the author reports parity for mid/large memcpy, memset and memcmp, and glibc ahead on strlen (0.5-0.8x) and strstr (0.4-0.65x); no per-size table is published
Allocations above 4080 bytes: each gets its own mmap/munmap under a global spinlock, a syscall per malloc and per free; the benchmark only covers 8-1024 byte blocks

Long-running processes with phase changes: small-run memory is never returned to the kernel, and up to 1 MiB of thread-cached blocks is stranded per exiting thread unless asm_alloc_flush_tcache() is called from a thread-exit hook

Pre-Haswell or FMA-less x86-64: the IFUNC fallback covers only the memory/string/search routines; the math objects in libasmlib.a/.so are compiled with -msse4.1 -mfma (use libasmlib_scalar.a there); macOS/BSD have no heap backend

Production code that needs a track record: the repository is ten days old (2026-09-27 to 2026-10-06, 31 commits, 0 stars, no releases on the GitHub page), and the AArch64 port is tested only under QEMU with no published hardware numbers

integration.dependencies: none at run time (Linux syscalls for the heap); build needs NASM 2.14+ and a C compiler (GNU as for AArch64, clang wasm32 target for wasm)
integration.min_toolchain: NASM 2.14+ (3.02 tested), C11 GCC or Clang; Makefile or CMake; IFUNC dispatch needs hosted Linux x86-64 with GCC/Clang
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux (AVX2/BMI hot paths with scalar IFUNC fallback; math requires FMA), AArch64 Linux (NEON), wasm32 and other freestanding targets via the portable C backend
integration.thread_safety: string/memory routines reentrant; asm_malloc thread-safe via per-thread cache plus a global spinlock (not async-signal-safe); arena single-threaded by design. The asm_alloc doc block in asmlib.h still says the allocator is single-threaded, contradicting the README and alloc.asm.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — asm_* names by default; ASMLIB_ENABLE_LIBC_ALIASES macro-maps the string, ctype, printf, qsort and aligned-allocation names in one translation unit, but malloc/calloc/realloc/free stay libc and asm_malloc pointers must never reach libc free

gotchas: Harness flaw found this session (bench/arena_bench.c): the glibc side frees whole bursts of 1 KiB (2048 blocks, 2 MiB) and mixed 8-512 B blocks (4000, about 1 MB) each trial, which with glibc's default 128 KiB M_TRIM_THRESHOLD should hand the heap top back to the kernel and re-fault it next trial, while the arena reuses one pre-faulted 4 MiB mmap buffer and asm_malloc never returns small runs. The glibc 2048 x 1 KiB row costs 494 ns per malloc+free pair (derived from page data), 13x the 37.46 ns/op of the 64 B row, so the 45.46x, 19.80x and 8.08x rows largely measure page faults and brk trimming rather than allocator code; the 64 B rows (8.59x arena, 4.79x heap) are the cleaner comparison. Inferred from the harness and glibc defaults, not re-run here.

ASMLIB_ENABLE_LIBC_ALIASES maps aligned_alloc, posix_memalign, reallocarray, malloc_usable_size and asprintf/vasprintf to the asm heap but leaves free, malloc and realloc on libc, so ordinary code such as aligned_alloc(...)/free(p) or asprintf(&s, ...)/free(s) in an aliased file hands an asm_malloc pointer to libc free, which asmlib.h itself says must never happen; asm_free does no pointer validation outside ASMLIB_ALLOC_DEBUG.

Published numbers lag the code: the snprintf table (1.53-2.10x) measured the hand-written asm_snprintf that CHANGELOG [Unreleased] removed on 2026-10-06; the current asm_snprintf is the portable C printf engine and is unmeasured. The memchr harness always hits 'z' at offset 25, memcmp compares a buffer with itself (asm_memcmp has no pointer-equality shortcut, so this is an equal-input full scan, not an invalid row), strstr searches for an absent "zzz", and memmem has no benchmark despite the 'several times faster' claim.

The math library is musl-derived portable C, not assembly; against glibc 2.44 only cbrt (2.18x), asinh (1.38x) and cosh (1.33x) are clearly faster and 13 of the 18 published functions are slower (sinh 0.52x).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over FastMemcpy, memcpy_benchmark or ademakov/bzero when you want a tested, whole libc subset (strings, allocators, formatting, wasm build) rather than a single faster memcpy or memset; for raw memcpy/memset speed against a current glibc it shows only parity, so none of these is a clear win there.
verified_claims_summary: Author's best-of-7 to 9 laptop runs on an Intel i7-10510U with glibc 2.44 (harness -O2; whether GCC 16.2.1 or Clang 22.1.8 built it is unstated): arena 4.36 vs 37.46 ns per op against malloc/free for 1000 x 64 B (8.59x), asm_malloc 8.55 vs 40.94 ns (4.79x), asm_sscanf 2.2-3.1x and asm_u64toa 3.98x over glibc, libm mostly slower. The larger 19.8x, 8.08x and 45x allocator rows probably include glibc returning freed memory to the kernel between trials, and the memory/string results are reported only as ranges at or below parity except memchr.
status_note: Active but brand-new (first commit 2026-09-27, last 2026-10-06, v1.0.0 in CHANGELOG, 0 stars); MIT with musl-derived math under MIT, thorough differential, guard-page, sanitizer and fuzz tests, but no external users or independent numbers yet.
